opus-5.5.text:
I think the answer really depends on what you want the model to do for you, and whether pre-training is actually your bottleneck.

A few years ago the logic was simple: whoever had the best base model won, because almost everything downstream inherited from it. Today it's more nuanced. Pre-training is still the foundation. It determines how much world knowledge and raw capability the model has. But a lot of the differentiation now comes from post-training, reinforcement learning, and especially from how you connect the model to real tasks, real environments, and real users.

So when a company asks, "Should we invest in pre-training again?", I'd ask three questions.

First, **is there a capability gap you can't close any other way?** If your product needs something the available base models fundamentally lack, maybe a modality, a language, a domain, or some property like long context or efficiency, then pre-training might be the right lever. If the gap is really about behavior, alignment with your use case, or agentic skills, RL and post-training are often much cheaper and faster.

Second, **do you have a differentiated advantage in data or compute?** Pre-training is a scale game. If you're just going to do what the leading labs do with less compute and the same internet data, it's hard to see the return. But if you have unique data, unique user interactions, or a very different objective, that changes the calculation.

Third, **what's the strategic value of owning the whole stack?** For some companies, controlling the base model matters for cost, for iteration speed, for not being dependent on someone else's roadmap. That's not purely a technical question. It's a business and organizational one. And having a pre-training team also builds a kind of deep understanding of models that's hard to get otherwise.

My personal view is that we're moving into what I'd call the second half of AI. The first half was about building better models and better methods, climbing benchmarks. The second half is more about defining the right problems and evaluations, and about utility: does the model actually create value in the real world? In that framing, pre-training is still essential infrastructure, but it's not automatically where the marginal dollar should go. You should invest in it when it's clearly the thing standing between you and the utility you want to deliver. Otherwise, your effort is often better spent on environments, tasks, RL, and product.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training is hard to justify when a company has less compute and the same internet data, but it does not explain that access to open-source models or APIs reduces the value of doing its own pre-training.

r002.rationale: It describes post-training as a source of differentiation and a way to improve behavior, but does not state that post-training is required to realize pre-training’s value.

r003.rationale: It says pre-training may be the right investment when a product has a capability gap available base models cannot fill, and that investment makes sense when pre-training is what stands between the company and its desired utility.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the question itself has shifted. Two or three years ago, "should we pre-train" basically meant "should we spend a lot of money to replicate what OpenAI did." Today the real question is different: what are you actually trying to get out of the base model that you can't get any other way?

So my framework is roughly three things.

First, do you have a differentiated data or compute advantage? Pre-training is fundamentally a game of scale and data. If you're training on the same internet data as everyone else, with less compute, you're going to converge to something slightly worse than what already exists, and you'll have spent a huge amount to get there. But if you have proprietary data — code from your own ecosystem, long-horizon interaction traces, domain data that genuinely isn't on the open web — then the base model you train can be meaningfully different, not just slightly behind.

Second, do you need control over the model for what comes after? This is the part people underestimate. A lot of the interesting progress right now isn't in pre-training per se, it's in post-training and RL — agents, long-horizon tasks, tool use. But those methods often depend on things in the base model: what mid-training data it saw, how it handles long context, whether the representations are amenable to the kind of RL you want to do. If you're only using someone else's API or weights, you're limited to what they decided to bake in. So sometimes pre-training is really a bet on being able to do post-training well, and that's a legitimate reason.

Third, and this is more strategic: are you willing to pay the cost of staying in the game, not just entering it? One model isn't a strategy. The frontier moves every six months. If you pre-train once and then can't keep up, you've basically bought a very expensive snapshot that depreciates quickly. So the real question for a company is whether the organization can sustain that iteration — talent, infra, the willingness to keep burning money while the return is uncertain.

Where I come out is that for most companies, the honest answer is no, it doesn't make sense to do frontier pre-training. Open-weight models are good enough that the marginal value you'd add is small relative to the cost. The leverage is in the second half — RL, environments, evaluation, products that generate the data that make the model better. That's where I'd put the money.

But for a small number of players who have real data moats and the appetite to stay in it for years, I think it's actually becoming more rational, not less. Because as the paradigm shifts toward agents and RL, the base model matters in new ways, and whoever controls it controls what's possible on top of it. So it's not "pre-training is dead," it's more that pre-training has become a means to an end rather than the end itself. And you should invest in it only if you're clear about what that end is.

r001.rationale: The response says open-weight models are good enough that a company’s marginal value from frontier pre-training is small relative to its cost, and notes that relying on another provider’s API or weights limits control.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training can be a bet on doing post-training well, and identifies post-training and RL as where much of the current progress and leverage lie.

r003.rationale: It describes pre-training as worthwhile for players with differentiated data or a need to shape the base model for later agents and RL, provided they can sustain the cost and have a clear purpose.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what is making pre-training unattractive today. Is it that we’ve reached a fundamental limit, or that the next increment of capability costs more than a company can justify? Those are different problems.

For an individual company, the question is whether pre-training gives you something important that you can’t get by taking an existing model and improving it through post-training or building a better system around it. If your main bottleneck is getting a model to complete a particular workflow reliably, another large pre-training run might not be the most effective investment. But if the bottleneck is a basic capability that existing models don’t have, then investing further upstream could make sense.

I’d also look at whether the company has a specific hypothesis about what will improve: better data, a different training objective, a different architecture. ‘We have more compute, so let’s train a bigger model’ needs a convincing expected return.

So I wouldn’t judge it just by whether pre-training loss keeps going down. I’d ask whether that improvement translates into useful capabilities, and whether the company can capture enough value from those capabilities to justify the cost.

r001.rationale: The response considers improving an existing model as an alternative to pre-training, but does not explain that access to open-source models or APIs reduces the value of doing pre-training in-house.

r002.rationale: Post-training is mentioned as a way to improve an existing model, but the response does not state that realizing pre-training’s value requires subsequent post-training.

r003.rationale: The response says useful capabilities should justify pre-training’s cost, but does not connect that case to meeting distinct requirements of future applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether pre-training is still the bottleneck for the product you want to build. A stronger base model can improve many downstream tasks, but that doesn’t automatically make training one yourself a good investment.

I’d look at three things: whether additional pre-training produces meaningful gains on the tasks your users care about; whether you have an advantage in data, compute, or research that makes those gains economical; and whether you can capture enough value to justify the cost compared with using an existing model.

For example, if your agent fails because it lacks certain knowledge or reasoning capabilities, better pre-training might help. If it fails because it cannot get the right information, use tools reliably, or learn from feedback, then retrieval, post-training, or improvements to the agent system may be a better investment.

So I wouldn’t make it a general bet that pre-training is back or that pre-training is over. I’d ask: what capability are we missing, and what is the cheapest reliable way to obtain it?

r001.rationale: It compares training a model with using an existing one, but does not say that access to open-source models or APIs reduces the incremental value of doing pre-training.

r002.rationale: It mentions post-training as a possible alternative when an agent has certain failures, but does not state that realizing pre-training’s value requires subsequent post-training.

r003.rationale: It says pre-training may help when it improves capabilities needed for a product’s user tasks, and that the gains and captured value must justify the cost.
